title: Why Wildfires Spread
objective: After this level you can explain how heat, drought, wind and fuel combine to drive a wildfire and a longer fire season.
summary: Fire needs heat, oxygen and fuel; a wildfire's behavior depends on fuels, weather and slope. Western fire seasons are over a month longer, as warming meets fuel built up by suppression.

cards.headline: A wildfire usually runs faster uphill than down.
cards.body: Fire needs only three ingredients to start. How far and fast a wildfire spreads depends on three more. Learn both, and a fire forecast starts to make sense.

cards.headline: Two triangles
cards.body: The fire triangle is heat, oxygen and fuel: what any fire needs to burn. Firefighters add a second, the fire behavior triangle: fuels, weather and topography, the shape of the land. The first triangle says whether something burns. The second says how a wildfire will behave once it does.

cards.headline: Fuel, weather, slope
cards.body: In fuel, moisture matters most. Living trees hold a lot of water and dead logs very little, and a fire must drive the water off before anything burns. Wind feeds the flames fresh oxygen and pushes them toward new fuel. Low humidity dries fuel out, so it catches faster and burns faster. And a wildfire typically runs faster uphill than downhill or on flat ground.

cards.headline: A longer fire season
cards.body: Looking back over 35 years of weather data, Forest Service scientists found fire seasons starting earlier in spring and running later into autumn. Parts of the western US now have seasons more than a month longer. NASA points to two things working together: a warming climate (hotter weather, earlier snowmelt, warmer nights, less summer rain) and decades of fire suppression that let fuel pile up in some forests.

cards.headline: Wildfire: understood
learned: Fire needs heat, oxygen and fuel
Fuels, weather and slope drive spread
Wind feeds it; dry air dries its fuel
Longer seasons: warming plus built-up fuel

questions.prompt: What are the three legs of the fire behavior triangle?

options.label: Heat, oxygen and fuel
options.rationale: That's the fire triangle: what any fire needs to burn.

options.label: Wind, rain and lightning
options.rationale: Those are weather details, not the three legs.

options.label: Trees, grass and buildings
options.rationale: Those are all fuels, one leg of the triangle.

questions.explanation: The fire behavior triangle is fuels, weather and topography; the fire triangle is heat, oxygen and fuel.

questions.prompt: One person blames bigger western fires only on forest management; another blames only climate. What does NASA's account suggest?

options.label: Only fuel buildup; climate plays no part
options.rationale: NASA also lists hotter weather, earlier snowmelt and less summer rain.

options.label: Both: built-up fuel plus warmer, drier conditions
Only climate; the amount of fuel doesn't matter
options.rationale: Decades of suppression let fuel pile up in some forests.

options.label: Neither, since fire seasons haven't changed
options.rationale: Parts of the West now have seasons more than a month longer.

questions.explanation: NASA says a warming climate and fuel built up by decades of fire suppression work together to raise the potential for extreme fires.

questions.prompt: In Level 1's terms, which spheres supply a wildfire's fuel and the wind that feeds it oxygen?

options.label: The geosphere and the hydrosphere
options.rationale: Rock doesn't burn, and water in fuel slows a fire.

options.label: The hydrosphere and the atmosphere
options.rationale: Wind is atmosphere, but the fuel is living and dead plants.

options.label: Only the geosphere, where the fire burns
options.rationale: The fuel is plants, and the oxygen comes from the air.

questions.explanation: Trees and dead wood are part of the biosphere; wind and oxygen come from the atmosphere.
